e.etymology: A respelling of Madeline shaped by Lynn. Madeline comes through French Madeleine from Magdalene, the byname of Mary Magdalene, meaning of Magdala, a village on the Sea of Galilee.
From Spanish and Italian alba, dawn, which goes back to Latin albus, white. It is a top girls' name in Spain.

assoc.t: Alba, the Scottish Gaelic name for Scotland
Italian town famous for white truffles

e.etymology: The English word, from Old French jouel, used as a given name since the late 19th century alongside Pearl, Ruby and Opal.
namesakes: Jewel (singer-songwriter of Who Will Save Your Soul)

assoc.t: jewel, the everyday word for a precious gem

e.etymology: From the place name: the Channel Island of Jersey and the state of New Jersey named after it. The island's name is Norse, ending in ey, island; the word for a sports shirt comes from its knitwear.

assoc.t: New Jersey, often called just Jersey
Jersey, island in the English Channel

e.etymology: A modern American name close in sound to Aiden, Avery and Evan. It also exists as a surname of Norwegian origin.
From the Arabic root z-y-n, beauty and adornment, the same root as Zayn. It is popular in South Asian Muslim families.
From the cattleya orchid, a genus named in 1824 for the English horticulturist William Cattley. As a baby name it took off in the form Cataleya after the 2011 film Colombiana.

assoc.t: genus of showy orchids, the classic corsage orchid

e.note: The spelling begins with the word cattle, which invites misreading; Cataleya is the more common spelling of the name.

e.etymology: From the Arabic root z-h-r, which covers both blossoming and shining, the same root as Zahra. A Hebrew name of the same shape, related to zohar, means radiance.
namesakes: Zahara Jolie (daughter of Angelina Jolie and Brad Pitt)

e.etymology: A modern American name that puts a V on the sound of Ada, Jayda and Kayda; compare the older Vada. It also exists as a surname from Hungarian vajda, a military governor.
A spelling of Everly, an English surname and place name from Old English eofor (wild boar) plus leah (woodland clearing).
A spelling of Layla, from Arabic layla, night. Hebrew laylah also means night, and Lailah is the angel of night and conception in Jewish legend.
A short form of Sebastian, from Latin Sebastianus, a man from the city of Sebaste, whose name comes from Greek sebastos, venerable.
namesakes: Bastian Bux (boy hero of The NeverEnding Story)
Bastian Schweinsteiger (German World Cup-winning soccer star)

assoc.t: Bastian, the boy reader in The NeverEnding Story

e.etymology: Popularized by Wendy Darling in J. M. Barrie's Peter Pan (1904). Barrie took it from fwendy-wendy, a small child's way of calling him friend. It was also an occasional pet form of Gwendolen.
namesakes: Wendy Darling (girl who flies to Neverland in Peter Pan)

e.etymology: A modern spelling of Hailey, an English surname and place name from Old English heg (hay) plus leah (clearing, meadow).
namesakes: Hailee Steinfeld (actress and singer, True Grit and Hawkeye)

e.etymology: A spelling of Jade, perhaps influenced by Jay. The stone's name comes from Spanish piedra de ijada, stone of the flank, because it was thought to cure kidney pain.
The Portuguese form of James. It arose when Santiago (Saint James, from Sant Iago) was reread as San Tiago. James goes back through Latin and Greek to Hebrew Ya'aqov, Jacob.
From the German occupational surname Decker, a roofer or thatcher, from decken, to cover.
The Spanish, Catalan and Slavic form of Ariadne, from Greek ari (most) plus a Cretan word for holy. In myth Ariadne gave Theseus the thread that led him out of the Labyrinth.
namesakes: Ariadne (Cretan princess who helped Theseus escape the Labyrinth)

e.etymology: Usually explained as Hebrew, from a root meaning noble or majestic. Adhara, also spelled Adara, is a bright star in Canis Major whose Arabic name means maidens. The name is well used in Spain.

assoc.t: Adhara, a bright star in Canis Major

e.etymology: A spelling of Robin, a medieval pet form of Robert, from Germanic words for fame and bright. As a girls' name it is also linked to the bird.
namesakes: Robyn (Swedish pop singer of Dancing on My Own)

e.etymology: From a Visigothic name Latinized as Ranamirus. The second element means famous; the first is read as wedge or as counsel. Several medieval kings of Leon and Aragon bore it.
From Basque maite, love or beloved. In Spanish it is also a contraction of Maria Teresa.
namesakes: Maite Perroni (Mexican actress and RBD singer)
e.note: English speakers tend to read it as MATE or MAY-tee; the Spanish and Basque sound is MY-tay.

e.etymology: From the English surname and place name, Old English hramsa (wild garlic) plus ieg (island). Ramsay is the Scottish spelling of the same name.

assoc.t: chef Gordon Ramsay, by surname (spelled Ramsay)
Dave Ramsey, personal finance radio host, by surname
JonBenet Ramsey murder case of 1996, by surname
Ramsay Bolton, Game of Thrones villain

e.etymology: A K spelling of Caius, a form of the Roman first name Gaius, as in Gaius Julius Caesar. The meaning of the Latin name is uncertain. Kaius also works as a longer form of Kai.
A short name with several sources: a Greek pet form of Anastasia, an Indian name used as a form of Siya (Sita), and a clipping of names ending in -sia.
namesakes: Sia (Australian pop singer of Chandelier and Cheap Thrills)

assoc.t: Australian pop singer Sia of Chandelier

e.meaning: who is like God?; in Japanese it depends on the characters
e.etymology: Three names share the spelling: a Japanese girls' name written with characters such as beautiful and fragrance, a Finnish short form of Mikael, and a variant of the biblical Micah.
namesakes: Mika (British pop singer of Grace Kelly)

e.etymology: Made famous by the actress Farrah Fawcett and usually taken as a spelling of Arabic Farah, joy. Farrah is also an English surname, a variant of Farrar, an ironworker.
namesakes: Farrah Fawcett (Charlie's Angels star and 1970s icon)

e.etymology: A modern American extension of Max with the -ton ending of Paxton and Jaxton. Maxton is also a Scottish place name and surname meaning the settlement of a man named Maccus.
A recent American coinage with the -mir ending of Amir, Jamir and Samir, in the same family as Zamir and Zyaire.
An Irish-looking respelling of Megan, the Welsh pet form of Margaret, which comes from Greek margarites, pearl. The gh spelling looks Irish but is not an Irish form.
namesakes: Meghan Trainor (singer of All About That Bass)

e.etymology: From the English surname, first a nickname for someone with gray hair, and from the color word itself. Grey is the British spelling.
A feminine elaboration of Daria or Dario with the -ana ending, used mainly in Spanish-speaking families. Those names go back to the Persian royal name Darius.
